title: Only the ones that matter
briefing: ~/hosts has one file per server. A non-empty file means the host reported
in (it's up); an empty file means silence (it's down).
Build the roster of who's up: for each host, test whether its file has
content, and if so, record its name.
tips: Combine a loop with a test: `for h in *; do if [ -s "$h" ]; then ...; fi; done`.
`[ -s FILE ]` is true when FILE exists and is non-empty. Append a name with `echo "$h" >> ~/up.txt`.
objective: For every file in ~/hosts, if it is non-empty, append its name to ~/up.txt — so ~/up.txt lists exactly the hosts that are up.
expert_objective: Write the non-empty hosts in ~/hosts into ~/up.txt.
hints: Loop over the files and test each: `for h in *; do if [ -s "$h" ]; then ...; fi; done`.
`[ -s "$h" ]` is true only when the file has content. Inside the `then`, record it: `echo "$h" >> ~/up.txt`.
`cd ~/hosts`, then `for h in *; do if [ -s "$h" ]; then echo "$h" >> ~/up.txt; fi; done`.
solution:
cd ~/hosts
for h in *; do if [ -s "$h" ]; then echo "$h" >> ~/up.txt; fi; done
explanation: `if COND; then ...; fi` runs the body only when COND succeeds (exits 0). The condition here is `test` (spelled `[ ... ]`): `-s` asks 'does this file have content?'. A loop that makes a decision per item is the heart of almost every real script.
